Mean, variance, skewness and kurtosis (C backend)

Source: R/core_stats.R
cmom.Rd

The four standard descriptive moments of a numeric vector – where it is centred, how spread out it is, whether it leans to one side and how heavy its tails are – in one call to the compiled core. These are the four numbers a data description or a drift check usually reports together.

Usage

cmom(x)

Arguments

x

Numeric (or logical) vector; coerced with as.numeric().

Value

A named length-4 numeric vector: mean (units of x), variance (squared units of x, n - 1 denominator), skewness and kurtosis (both unitless; kurtosis as excess over the normal's 3).

Details

The mean is base R's (an extended-precision sum followed by a corrective pass); the deviations from it are then divided by their largest magnitude before any power is taken, and the scale is restored at the end. That avoids both the cancellation of the textbook “sum of squares minus square of sum” formula and overflow of fourth powers for values beyond about \(10^{77}\). It reads the data three times (mean, largest deviation, moments), in \(O(n)\) time. The variance uses the n - 1 denominator, matching stats::var(). The shape statistics use the sample moment definitions $$g_1 = m_3 / m_2^{3/2}, \qquad g_2 = m_4 / m_2^2 - 3,$$ with \(m_k = n^{-1} \sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^k\), so kurtosis is reported as EXCESS kurtosis: a normal sample sits near zero, not near three. These are the uncorrected moment ratios (type 1 in the classification of Joanes and Gill, 1998), not the bias-adjusted versions some software reports.

Edge cases are NaN, never an error: an empty vector gives four NaN; one value gives its mean and NaN for the rest; skewness needs at least 3 values and kurtosis at least 4; any NA or NaN in x makes every entry NaN. A constant vector has variance 0 and NaN shape statistics. A character, factor or list x is refused ("must be numeric").

References

Joanes DN, Gill CA (1998). Comparing measures of sample skewness and kurtosis. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series D (The Statistician) 47(1), 183–189. doi:10.1111/1467-9884.00122

See also

csdev(), cqnt() and cmad() for robust alternatives that one extreme value cannot move.

Examples

cmom(c(2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9))
#>      mean  variance  skewness  kurtosis 
#>  5.000000  4.571429  0.656250 -0.218750 

# The first two entries agree with base R.
m <- cmom(1:10)
all.equal(m[["mean"]], mean(1:10))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(m[["variance"]], stats::var(1:10))
#> [1] TRUE

# A symmetric sample has no skew; excess kurtosis is near 0 for normal
# data and positive for a heavy-tailed sample.
cmom(c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2))[["skewness"]]
#> [1] 0
cmom(c(rep(0, 20), -8, 8))[["kurtosis"]] > 0
#> [1] TRUE

# Too short to define a shape statistic: NaN rather than a guess.
cmom(c(1, 2))
#>     mean variance skewness kurtosis 
#>      1.5      0.5      NaN      NaN
